text.p: Car companies seeking to avoid look-alike television commercials for look-alike cars are spending big money on glitzy, surreal advertising that sometimes doesn't even show the vehicle.
Industry experts say a growing number of American and British car ads no longer focus on technical details but on the "personality" of the brand.

Last year 500 million pounds ($814.3 million) was spent on advertising cars on British television. The images used are becoming increasingly surreal in a bid to attract the attention of viewers dulled by similar-looking campaigns.

Industry sources say the new trend is emerging because there is now little to distinguish one car brand from another. But some also warn that consumers, while enjoying the ads, may forget the product.
British car ads have traditionally featured a winding road, beautiful scenery, a glamorous couple and haunting soundtrack with some technical detail thrown in for good measure.
"Because it is all aspirational much of the advertising is overtly status-ridden and packed with sterotypes," a spokesman for ad agency Publicis, which runs the Renault account, told Reuters.
But things are changing.
Ford's latest campaign for its Fiesta includes shots of an old man bouncing on a trampoline and a man blowing bubble-gum. It offers only a glimpse of the car in the final frame.
The launch of Ford's innovative Ka marque last year showed a lighthouse, a pair of feet and a bumble bee, but no car.
Simon Binns, account director at Ford's ad agency Ogilvy & Mather, said: "To appeal to ad literate (consumers) the advertising had to be incredibly fresh and original."
It is a tactic that has also been adopted by Germany's BMW which has run an ad featuring a yellow rubber duck with the BMW logo instead of eyes.

"Cars are becoming more and more similar. The technical differences are fewer and fewer and so the perceived image of the car becomes the biggest differentiating factor," said Chris Wood, chairman of branding company CLK.
His view is supported by Simon Mottram, a director of international branding group Interbrand.
"It's a huge trend for car makers to put personality into their brands. Cars used to be sold on their functional aspects. Now it's all about softer more expressive values," he said.
The Mini, which is made by Rover and which achieved cult status in the 1960s, is to be promoted as a fashion accessory in British style magazines this summer.
The ads will feature a range of brightly coloured customised cars which are almost hidden against a bright background.

"The Mini is a very individual brand and we want to emphasise that. If you drive one you can be cool, or trendy, or sporty or classic -- it allows you to express your own personality," said Paul Gordon, account director on the Mini brand at ad agency Ammirati Puris Lintas.
OTHER INNOVATIVE APPROACHES
While some British car ads have taken a surreal turn to promote the personality of the brand, others are pastiches of popular TV shows or glitzy Hollywood movies.
An advertisement for the Nissan Almera parodies the 1970s British police series "The Sweeney" and another for the Peugeot 106, has a story line loosely based on the movie "Thelma and Louise".
Ad industry experts say that while the ads are entertaining, many consumers have trouble remembering the product being advertised.

"We have found in research groups that although consumers enjoy the advertising they often can't remember who it was for. Which rather defeats the object," said Janet Bik, a director of branding specialist New Solutions.

Dave Trott, creative director of advertising agency Walsh Trott Chick Smith, said: "Do you remember the car ad with the soundtrack 'Search for the hero'? Beautifully shot, nicely edited, terrific song. But what was it for? Several million pounds later and all you're thinking is great soundtrack."
Trott said the problem with the ad for Peugeot and many others is "the advertisement becomes an end in itself and the selling of the product is forgotten."
Some industry experts believe car companies will come back to putting the cars and their technical details back into the ads.
"I think they (carmakers) will begin to tie the imagery more closely with the brand and use the car as the central hero of ad campaigns," said Bik.

"Ironically as car dealerships consolidate and their numbers decline, ads will be one of the places where consumers will actually be able to see what the cars look like," she said. ($ = 0.614 British Pounds)
